chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Haroun ibn Muslim, from Mas'ada, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), from his father (peace be upon him) who said:

Sudeyr came to my father (peace be upon him) during the month of Ramadan, and he said: 'O Sudeyr! Do you know which nights these are?' He said: 'Yes, may my father be sacrificed for you — these are the nights of the month of Ramadan. But what is that?' So he said to him: 'Are you able, during each night of these nights, to free ten slaves from the descendants of Ismail?' Sudeyr said to him: 'May my father and mother be sacrificed for you — my wealth does not amount to that.'

So he did not cease to reduce [the number] until he reached one slave. In each case he said: 'I am not able to do that.' Then he said to him: 'So are you able to provide the breaking of the fast for a Muslim man each night?' He said: 'Yes, and [even] ten.'

So my father (peace be upon him) said to him: 'That is what I intended, O Sudeyr! Your providing the breaking of the fast for your Muslim brother is equivalent to [freeing] one slave from the descendants of Ismail (peace be upon him).'

key_terms.إفطار: Breaking of the fast (iftar) — the evening meal with which the daily Ramadan fast is ended; providing this for another is a major charitable act
key_terms.رقبة: Neck — a Quranic metonym for a slave (from freeing the neck from bondage); used in fiqh texts for manumission
key_terms.وُلد إسماعيل: Children/descendants of Ismail — referring to the Arab tribes, historically associated with slavery in early Islamic law; freeing them was considered especially meritorious
key_terms.يعدل: Is equivalent to / equals — used here in the sense of spiritual equivalence in reward

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual reward of providing iftar for a fasting Muslim in Ramadan?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) taught Sudeyr, a close companion, that providing iftar (breaking the fast) for a fasting Muslim during Ramadan carries a reward equivalent to freeing one of the descendants of Ismail — an act considered among the most meritorious in Islamic tradition. The Imam employed a skillful pedagogical method: starting with an act far beyond Sudeyr's means (freeing ten slaves per night) and progressively reducing until he demonstrated that even the ordinary Muslim could perform an equivalent virtue through feeding a fellow believer. This dialogue illustrates the Islamic principle that acts of charity and brotherhood are spiritually elevated during Ramadan.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from Haroun Bin Muslim, from Mas’ada, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, from his<sup>asws</sup> father<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘Sudeyr came over to my<sup>asws</sup> father<sup>asws</sup> during the Month of Ramazan, so he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘O Sudeyr! Do you know which of the nights this one is?’ So he said, ‘Yes, may my father be sacrificed for you<sup>asws</sup>! These are the nights of the Month of Ramazan. So what is that?’ So he<sup>asws</sup> said to him: ‘Are you able upon freeing, during each night from these nights, ten necks from the children of Ismail<sup>as</sup>?’ So Sudeyr said to him: ‘May my father be sacrificed for you<sup>asws</sup>, and my mother (as well), my wealth would not reach that’.

So he<sup>asws</sup> did not cease to reduce (from ten) until it reached one neck. During each of that, he was saying, ‘I am not able over it’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘So what is your ability if you were to provide breaking of a Fast, during each night, to a Muslim man?’ So he said to him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘Yes, and (even) ten’.

So my<sup>asws</sup> father<sup>asws</sup> said to him: ‘So that is what I<sup>asws</sup> intended, O Sudeyr! Your providing for the breaking of a Fast for your Muslim brother equates to (liberating) one neck from the children of Ismail<sup>as</sup>’.
en.sarwar: 4. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from Harun ibn Muslim from Mas’adah from abu ‘Abd Allah, from his father, ‘Alayhim al-Salam, who has said the following:

“Once, during the month of Ramadan, Sadir went to visit abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam. The Imam asked, ‘O Sadir, do you know which nights are these days?’ He replied, ‘Yes, I pray to Allah to keep my soul and the soul of my father in service for your cause, these are the nights of the month of Ramadan, but what do they signify?’ The Imam then said, ‘Can you set free ten slaves from the descendants of Isma‘il in every one of these nights?’ Sadir replied, ‘I pray to Allah to keep the souls of my parents in service for your cause, my belongings are not that much.’

The Imam then reduced the number of slaves until it was only one slave, but he kept saying, ‘My belongings are not enough.’ The Imam then asked, ‘Can you serve food to a Muslim every night.’ He replied, ‘Yes, I can do so. I can even serve food to ten people every night.’
The Imam then said, ‘That is what I meant, O Sadir. Your serving food to your Muslim brother is equal in reward to setting free of ten slaves from the descendants of Isma‘il.’”
